proposed_edges.relationship: Hegel’s World-history criticised as a statist, Eurocentric frame, which in Guha’s words as Michael quotes them reached India “as an instrument of the East India Company’s colonial project”, and historians asked to learn from literature the “historicality” of everyday life (2002), as his reviewers and Chakrabarty read the book; Michael finds the argument “mostly confined to the conceptual level”
proposed_edges.map_label: Against Hegel’s World-history, 2002 (as reviewers read it)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: History at the Limit of World-History (Columbia University Press, 2002) is unread; its argument is given as its readers state it. Bernardo A. Michael (Journal of World History 15:4, 2004, pp. 530–532, read in full): lectures given at the Italian Academy at Columbia; Guha "takes the German philosopher Georg Hegel and his conception of 'World-History' (Weltgeschichte) to task" (p. 530); he quotes Guha that "World-History made its way to the subcontinent as an instrument of the East India Company's colonial project and helped it set up the Raj" (book p. 51) and that history should be "a call for historicality to be rescued from its containment in World-History" (book p. 6). Michael places the book among "recent postcolonial efforts to rethink the practices of disciplinary history and thereby provincialize its European lineages" (p. 532), and objects that "losing sight of the state at the level of the everyday might mean the loss of it as an object of critique", that "Guha's arguments are mostly confined to the conceptual level", and that Guha "seems to attribute to Hegel's World-History an agency that is hard to locate in the historicality of the colonial world" (p. 532). The Company connection is therefore Guha's claim as Michael reports it, and Michael doubts that the book demonstrates how Hegel's ideas became colonial practice. The publisher's description: World-history "reduces the course of human history to the amoral record of states and empires"; historians "should learn from literature"; Tagore's critique of historiography. Chakrabarty (Australian Academy of the Humanities obituary, 2024, read in full) calls it "a grand statement about literature being a far better communicator of senses of the past in the Indian subcontinent than the European discipline of history that had come to India as a practice of the colonial state" and "his farewell to the discipline of history". The theme is older: Chakraborty (2000, read in full) reports that Dominance without Hegemony (1997) already charged colonial historiography with the Hegelian view "that precolonial India had no state, therefore no history" (p. 376). A contribution to the postcolonial critique of historicism alongside Chakrabarty's provincializing argument (edge_914), not a claim that Guha belongs to a school; edge_115 (subaltern → post) records the group.

proposed_edges.relationship: Vivek Chibber: Dominance without Hegemony rests on “a highly mythologized story” of the English and French bourgeois revolutions, so its contrast between India’s bourgeoisie and Europe’s fails (2013–14); Sewell and Steinmetz accept the critique of Guha’s Europe, while Chatterjee, as Chibber reports him, denies that Guha made claims about those revolutions
proposed_edges.map_label: Chibber’s critique of Dominance without Hegemony, 2013–14
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from comparative historical sociology because his case is a comparison of the European bourgeois revolutions with Indian independence, and because his readers here include historical sociologists (Sewell is already a critic on this roster). Chibber's own words, read in part: Guha's work is "foundational for the entire Subalternist project" and "fundamentally flawed", because its "contrastive claims about the Indian bourgeoisie and Indian capitalism ... rest on a comparison with the European achievement", and "Guha quite dramatically misunderstands the European story" (response to Chatterjee, Verso, 25 February 2014); Guha's break between the bourgeoisies of West and East "flows from a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions, one that was rejected decades ago by historians" (JWSR 20:2, 2014, p. 313). Guha's words appear only as Chibber quotes them (Dominance without Hegemony, p. 19: the bourgeoisie's "historic triumphs in England in 1648 and France in 1789"; p. 5). Readers in the JWSR symposium: William H. Sewell Jr. (pp. 300–303, read in full) calls Guha's portrayal of the two revolutions "standard-issue orthodox Marxism—and ... well past its 'sell-by' date" (p. 301) while finding Chibber's own history "a bit shaky"; George Steinmetz (p. 284) writes that "Guha was relying on a version of Marxist political theory and German history that was demolished by the critics of the Sonderweg thesis"; Bruce Cumings finds the critique "persuasive, at least at the level of how one defines hegemony" (p. 290) but says "I don't know Guha's work" (p. 292), so Chibber's claim that all the critics accepted his reading of Guha (p. 313) is not adopted here. The defence: at the Historical Materialism conference (New York, April 2013) and in a written reply, Partha Chatterjee argued, as Chibber reports him, that Guha made no claims about the classic bourgeois revolutions and criticised only the historiography of colonial India; Chatterjee's text is unread. Chibber's book (Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital, Verso, 2013) is unread; its focus on Guha and Chakrabarty is from Hung's introduction (p. 281). The endpoint locates the intervention; it does not make the critique the field's verdict.

proposed_edges.relationship: A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) traces the Permanent Settlement to the mercantilist, physiocratic and classical political economy of East India Company officials, as Bhambra reads it; she faults its neglect of the colonial context (2024)
proposed_edges.map_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal, 1963 (as Bhambra reads it)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A repair to the pre-2000 core. The book (Paris: Mouton, 1963) is unread; it is known through its readers. Gurminder K. Bhambra (Discover Society, 2024, read in full): the book addresses the late-eighteenth-century debates among East India Company administrators over a "permanent settlement", and Guha "set out their different economic premises – deriving from mercantilist, physiocratic, and classical political economy – and demonstrated that, despite their differences, they nonetheless shared a common political focus, establishing the permanence of orderly dominion"; she quotes his p. 9 on entrusting revenue to "a class of native entrepreneurs who had solid interests in the land and were politically reliable". Her criticism: "his failure to locate the discussions of the East India Company administrators within their colonial context". She reports, without these being read here, Sarvepalli Gopal's 1966 view of the book as "primarily ... an exercise in British intellectual history" and Guha's answer in the 1981 preface to the second edition. Holmwood's editorial (2024) calls it "a major contribution to the history of political economy"; Chakrabarty (2024) writes that it "showed an early awareness of the importance of ideas in economic history". A contribution to the history of economic ideas in colonial policy; no claim is made about the book's reception by economists.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: A single hostile review by a reviewer identified only by place; kept in the description and chronology.
The 2002 book criticises Hegel’s philosophical concept of World-history, not the world/global history field.
Michael’s comparison with Lefebvre and Certeau is a reviewer’s association, not Guha’s claim.
edge_976 records the 1982–83 programme; the later book goes to post.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. The book "grew out of a series of lectures delivered by Ranajit Guha ... at the Italian Academy for Advanced Studies in America at Columbia University" (p. 530); Guha "takes the German philosopher Georg Hegel and his conception of 'World-History' (Weltgeschichte) to task" (p. 530). Guha quoted: history outside World-History is "a creative engagement with the past as a story of man's being in the everyday world. It is in short, a call for historicality to be rescued from its containment in World-History" (book p. 6); "World-History made its way to the subcontinent as an instrument of the East India Company's colonial project and helped it set up the Raj" (book p. 51). Praise: the book joins "a growing chorus of scholars" on everyday life (Lefebvre, Certeau, Goffman, Le Roy Ladurie) and is "definitely worth a read for those interested in ... recent postcolonial efforts to rethink the practices of disciplinary history and thereby provincialize its European lineages" (pp. 531–532). Criticism: "losing sight of the state at the level of the everyday might mean the loss of it as an object of critique"; "Guha's arguments are mostly confined to the conceptual level"; he "seems to attribute to Hegel's World-History an agency that is hard to locate in the historicality of the colonial world" (p. 532). The book itself is unread.

new_sources.title: Amalendu K. Chakraborty, review of Ranajit Guha, Dominance without Hegemony: History and Power in Colonial India, Journal of World History 11:2 (Fall 2000): 373–379.
new_sources.citation: Amalendu K. Chakraborty, review of Ranajit Guha, Dominance without Hegemony: History and Power in Colonial India, Journal of World History 11:2 (Fall 2000): 373–379.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. Reviews the Harvard University Press paperback, which he dates 1998. "A compilation of three interrelated essays", "an ideological critique of the South Asian colonial and nationalist state and its historiography from the perspective of Antonio Gramsci's philosophical reflections on 'hegemony' and 'domination'" (pp. 373–374). Reports Guha's argument that colonial historiography perpetuated "the prejudicial view, derived from the Hegelian view of history, that precolonial India had no state, therefore no history" (p. 376). Criticism: the absence of "the voices of the 'subalterns' themselves" reduces the project "to a mere armchair ideological 'discourse' on behalf of the subalterns" (p. 375); Guha "conveniently skips the portrayal of the Hindu social order in the Muslim historiography of India" (p. 377); "Guha's intellectual indebtedness to the Marxist-Leninist-Gramscian ideology of western European history does not allow him to examine Indian nationalist history from the perspective of Indian reality" (p. 379). He also calls Guha "a formidable Marxist historian" (p. 375). The reviewer is identified only by place (Minneapolis).

new_sources.title: Vivek Chibber, response to Partha Chatterjee ("Subaltern Studies Revisited"), with an introduction by Clément Petitjean, Verso, 25 February 2014.
new_sources.citation: Vivek Chibber, response to Partha Chatterjee ("Subaltern Studies Revisited"), with an introduction by Clément Petitjean, Verso, 25 February 2014.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.151: the introduction and the sections "Guha and the Bourgeois Revolutions" and "Does Guha refer to the bourgeois revolutions?". Petitjean: "In April 2013, at the annual Historical Materialism conference held in New York, Vivek Chibber appeared alongside Partha Chatterjee in a much-anticipated critical debate." Chibber: "I argue in PTSC that Guha's work is both foundational for the entire Subalternist project ... and that it is fundamentally flawed. Its flaw is that it generates a set of contrastive claims about the Indian bourgeoisie and Indian capitalism that rest on a comparison with the European achievement. But the comparison fails because Guha quite dramatically misunderstands the European story"; "the European bourgeoisie was no more committed to an integrated political culture than was its Indian counterpart". Chatterjee's three replies, as Chibber reports them (Chatterjee's text is unread): Guha makes no claims about the classic bourgeois revolutions, only about the historiography of colonial India; "Indian bourgeoisie" means the Congress's middle-class leadership; any European referent is the mid-twentieth-century British state. Chibber quotes Dominance without Hegemony p. 19 (the bourgeoisie's "historic triumphs in England in 1648 and France in 1789") and p. 5 (its "failure to measure up to the heroism of the European bourgeoisie in its period of ascendancy").

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. A historian of France with "only a passing acquaintance" with Indian history (p. 300). Guha's Dominance without Hegemony (1997) "was written from within a basically Marxist framework" (p. 300). On Guha's account of the English and French revolutions: "this portrayal ... is standard-issue orthodox Marxism—and is by now well past its 'sell-by' date" (p. 301). Chibber's "own grasp of French and English history seems to me a bit shaky" (no mention of 1688; liberal contributions called "weak"), "Nevertheless, Chibber's most important conclusions about the European experience seem to me quite correct" (p. 301). On Chakrabarty, pp. 301–302 (used in the Chakrabarty draft). Sums up the book as "a careful, sustained, intelligent, and salutary critique of Subaltern Studies" whose "genius is critique, however, rather than reconstruction" (p. 302).

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.151 (pp. 311–314). "Guha's argument for there being a historic break between the political projects of the bourgeoisie in the West and in the East flows from a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions, one that was rejected decades ago by historians" (p. 313). He writes that "All the critics in this forum accept both my reconstruction of Guha as well as my criticism of him" (p. 313); Cumings, in the same forum, says he does not know Guha's work. To Sewell: the revolutions' shifts "were nowhere near what is needed to validate Guha's argument", and movement towards inclusion came from "pressure from the laboring classes" (pp. 313–314). Also read (Spivak research pass): p. 311 and n. 1, where he answers Steinmetz that he focused on the historians and anthropologists of the field rather than theorists such as Spivak, and cites his reply to Spivak in the Cambridge Review of International Affairs (2014).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. On A Rule of Property for Bengal (Paris: Mouton, 1963): the debates among East India Company administrators over a "permanent settlement", entrusting revenue to "a class of native entrepreneurs who had solid interests in the land and were politically reliable" (Guha, p. 9, as she quotes); Guha "set out their different economic premises – deriving from mercantilist, physiocratic, and classical political economy – and demonstrated that, despite their differences, they nonetheless shared a common political focus, establishing the permanence of orderly dominion." She reports that Sarvepalli Gopal's 1966 review regarded it "primarily as an exercise in British intellectual history" and that Guha answered such critics in the 1981 preface to the second edition (both mediated through her). Her criticism: "his failure to locate the discussions of the East India Company administrators within their colonial context"; "the refusal to consider colonialism as central to the emergence and development of capitalism perhaps blunted the force of his arguments". The book is unread.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. A former doctoral student at the ANU. It was "often commented" that Subaltern Studies applied the history from below of Thompson, Rudé and Hobsbawm, but this missed that they "characterised their subjects as 'backward', and their forms of protest and rebellion as 'prepolitical'". He reads two reasons in Elementary Aspects, "in tension with each other", why peasant revolt was political. "This is the core idea underpinning his Dominance without Hegemony – that colonial capitalism and the colonial state integrated India into global capital and modern forms of statehood, but without establishing a hegemonic bourgeois culture." Cites the book as Harvard University Press, 1998.

new_sources.citation: Dipesh Chakrabarty, "Ranajit Guha FAHA 1923–2023," Australian Academy of the Humanities, May 2024 (Fellows' obituary).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. Honorary Fellow of the Academy, 1996; died in Vienna on 28 April 2023; left Canberra for Vienna in 1999; "edited the first six volumes of the series". A Rule of Property "showed an early awareness of the importance of ideas in economic history. He was clearly no votary of any kind of economic determinism." On the 2002 book (which he calls "History and the Limit of World History"): "a grand statement about literature being a far better communicator of senses of the past in the Indian subcontinent than the European discipline of history that had come to India as a practice of the colonial state"; "This book thus signaled his farewell to the discipline of history"; "He also bade goodbye to writing in English. In the last ten or fifteen years of his life, Guha wrote several books and essays in Bengali and went on to win a prestigious literary prize in Calcutta" (the prize and the books are not named). The writer was a member of the Subaltern Studies collective.
